chapters.prelude:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def topple_step(a, K=3):
    """One round of toppling: every cell above K sends 1 grain to each of 4 neighbours.
    Grains pushed past the edge fall off the table."""
    toppling = a > K
    n = toppling.sum()
    t = toppling.astype(a.dtype)
    a -= 4 * t
    a[1:, :] += t[:-1, :]
    a[:-1, :] += t[1:, :]
    a[:, 1:] += t[:, :-1]
    a[:, :-1] += t[:, 1:]
    return n

questions.q: city = np.array([1, 2, 0, 1]). What does np.mean(city == 1) give?

opts.t: 1, because the first house is red
0.5, the fraction of houses that are red
An error: you can't average booleans

questions.why: city == 1 is [True, False, False, True]. numpy treats True as 1 and False as 0, so the mean is 2/4 = 0.5. "Mean of a mask" = "fraction that satisfy the condition", a pattern you'll use in every chapter.

questions.q: Which pair best describes the move from classical models to the Schelling model?

opts.t: From one or two bodies described by equations, to many simple agents studied by simulation

questions.why: Classical physics models a few bodies with equations you can solve. Schelling's model has hundreds of agents with a simple rule, and the interesting result, strong clustering from mild preferences, appears only when you run it. That is the core shift complexity science describes.

questions.q: Nobody in the model wants a segregated street (at p = 0.5 everyone is fine with half their neighbours being different). Yet the street segregates. What is the name for a pattern at the level of the whole system that no individual rule mentions?
questions.why: Emergence: the system-level property (large single-colour blocks) is not written into any agent's rule. You saw it appear in the plot.

questions.q: In your own words: why does a city segregate strongly even when each household is happy with half its neighbours being different?
questions.a:
• A household that moves leaves a gap and lands somewhere new, which changes the neighbourhood of several other households.
  • Moves are local and keep cascading: each move can make a neighbour unhappy, who then moves too.
  • The system only stops when (almost) nobody is unhappy, and the configurations where nobody is unhappy are mostly clustered ones. Mild individual preferences + feedback = strong collective pattern.

questions.q: Why use np.roll instead of a loop with city[i-1] and city[i+1]?
questions.a:
• It handles the whole array at once (fast, short code).
  • It wraps around, so the ends of the street need no special case: the street is a ring.
  • np.roll(city, d) lines every house up with its neighbour at offset d, so one comparison checks every house.

questions.q: In an undirected graph with n nodes, how many edges does the complete graph (every node linked to every other) have?
questions.why: Each of the n nodes links to n-1 others, giving n(n-1) ends of edges, and every edge has two ends, so n(n-1)/2 edges. With 10 guests that's 45 conversations.

questions.title: reachable_nodes, the classic version
questions.prompt: Rebuild the search. A stack holds nodes we have found but not processed; seen holds nodes we've processed.

questions.code:
def reachable_nodes(G, start):
    seen = set()
    stack = [start]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node not in seen:
            seen.add(node)
            stack.extend(G.neighbors(node))
    return seen

G = nx.Graph([(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 5)])
print(sorted(reachable_nodes(G, 2)))
print(sorted(reachable_nodes(G, 5)))
print(len(G), len(reachable_nodes(G, 3)))

questions.q: In G(n, p) with n = 100 and p = 0.1, about how many edges do you expect?
questions.why: There are 100·99/2 = 4950 possible pairs and each is an edge with probability 0.1, so you expect 495.

questions.q: Explain how reachable_nodes works, and why it can't loop forever even though the graph has cycles.
questions.a:
• It keeps a stack of nodes still to process and a set of nodes already processed.
  • Each round it pops a node; if it's new it marks it seen and pushes all its neighbours.
  • Cycles lead back to nodes already in seen, which are popped and skipped, so each node is processed at most once and the loop ends when the stack is empty.
  • The graph is connected exactly when the set it returns contains every node.

questions.q: What happens to the probability that G(n, p) is connected as p increases, and what's special about ln(n)/n?
questions.a:
• It stays near 0 for small p, then jumps to near 1 over a narrow range of p: a phase transition.
  • The jump is centred near p\* = ln(n)/n, and it gets sharper as n grows.
  • Intuition: at p\*, the expected number of isolated nodes drops below about one; isolated nodes are the last thing stopping the graph from being connected.

questions.q: In a network where "my friends mostly know each other", what would you naively expect about the number of hand-offs between two random people?

opts.t: Very few, because everyone is tightly connected
Many, because messages keep circling inside local groups
It can't be estimated without the full network

questions.why: Local clustering means most of your links lead back into your own neighbourhood, so a purely local network has long paths. Milgram's short chains are the surprise this chapter explains.

questions.q: A ring lattice has n nodes, each with degree k. How many edges?
questions.why: Each node has k edge-ends and each edge has two ends, so n·k/2. The generator agrees: each node yields k/2 edges "to the right".

questions.q: Look at the plot around p = 0.01. What does a "small world" network have?

opts.t: Low clustering and short paths (a random graph)
High clustering and long paths (a lattice)

questions.why: A handful of shortcuts slashes the average path length (each shortcut serves many pairs), while clustering barely moves because almost every local triangle survives. Both properties at once is what Watts and Strogatz meant by small world.

questions.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2])
q.append(3)
q.appendleft(0)
print(q.popleft(), q.pop())
print(list(q))

questions.title: bfs, the classic way
questions.prompt: Rebuild BFS. Mark nodes as seen when they're queued, so nothing is queued twice.

questions.q: Explain why a few random shortcuts make paths short but leave clustering high.
questions.a:
• Path length is a global property: one shortcut between distant parts of the ring gives a fast route to everyone near either end, so the average over all pairs drops a lot.
  • Clustering is local: each shortcut destroys only the few triangles that used the edge it replaced. With p = 0.01, about 99% of edges, and almost all triangles, are untouched.
  • So there's a wide range of p where the network is both clustered (like a lattice) and short (like a random graph): a small world.

questions.q: What's the one change that turns depth-first search into breadth-first search, and why does BFS give shortest paths?
questions.a:
• Replace the stack (pop from the end) with a queue (pop from the front, deque.popleft).
  • BFS processes nodes in order of distance: all nodes at distance 1, then 2, and so on. So the first time a node is discovered, it's along a shortest path, and its distance is its parent's + 1.

questions.q: On log-log axes the BA degree PMF is roughly a straight line. What does that tell you?

opts.t: PMF(k) is roughly proportional to k raised to some negative power
All nodes have the same degree

questions.why: log PMF = −α log k + c is a straight line on log-log axes, which is the same as PMF(k) ∝ k^(−α): a power law. For the BA model α is about 3.

counts = {u: repeated.count(u) for u in set(repeated)}
print(counts)
print(round(counts[0] / len(repeated), 3))

questions.q: In the CCDF plot, the WS curve plunges to zero just past x ≈ 15, while BA's declines in a straight line out to the hundreds. In plain words?

opts.t: Both graphs have hubs, BA's are just bigger
In WS nobody has many more friends than average; in BA a few nodes have tens of times the average
WS has more edges than BA
The CCDF can't compare graphs with different k

questions.why: WS degrees are concentrated near the mean, so the CCDF drops off a cliff. BA's power-law tail means the chance of finding a node with degree above x falls slowly, so hubs exist.

questions.q: Why does the BA model produce hubs while the WS model doesn't? Mention both ingredients.
questions.a:
• WS starts from a lattice where every node has degree k and rewires a few edges, so degrees stay close to k.
  • BA has growth (old nodes have had more time to collect links) and preferential attachment (high-degree nodes are more likely to get the next link).
  • Together they create a feedback loop: being big makes you grow faster. The result is a power-law degree distribution with a few huge hubs.
  • Remove preferential attachment (uniform choice) and the tail becomes exponential: no hubs.

questions.q: What does the repeated_nodes list contain, and why does choosing from it uniformly implement preferential attachment?
questions.a:
• Every node appears in the list once for each edge it has (both ends of every edge get added).
  • So a node with degree d occupies d slots, and a uniform random pick lands on it with probability d / (total degree): proportional to degree.
  • It avoids computing probabilities explicitly; updating the list is just extend.

questions.q: How many different elementary CA rules are there?
questions.why: Each of the 8 neighbourhoods can map to 0 or 1, so there are 2⁸ = 256 rule tables, named Rule 0 to Rule 255.

bits = [(rule >> v) & 1 for v in range(8)]
print(bits)
print(format(rule, "08b"))

questions.tests:
assert a[2].tolist() == [0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0], f"Row 2 of Rule 30, got {a[2].tolist()}"
assert a[3].tolist() == [0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0], f"Row 3 of Rule 30, got {a[3].tolist()}"

questions.q: You run a rule from a random start and see triangles of all sizes, never settling, with no repeating pattern. Which class?
questions.why: Endless random-looking structure is Class 3, like Rule 30. Class 4 would show persistent "particles" moving through a regular background and colliding.

questions.q: What's surprising about Rule 30, given how it's built?

opts.t: It needs a random number generator to run
It's completely deterministic, yet its output passes many tests of randomness
It only works on wide rows
It produces a different picture each time from the same start

questions.why: Rule 30 has no randomness in it at all, yet from a single cell its centre column looks like coin flips. Mathematica used it as its random-number generator for years.

questions.q: Walk through how one row of an elementary CA is computed with numpy, from rule number to new row.
questions.a:
• Turn the rule number into an 8-entry table: bit v of the rule is the output for neighbourhood v.
  • For every cell, encode its neighbourhood as one number: 4·left + 2·self + 1·right. np.correlate(row, [4, 2, 1], mode="same") does this for the whole row.
  • Look up all cells at once: new_row = table[codes].

questions.q: What are Wolfram's four classes, and why is Class 4 the interesting one?
questions.a:
• 1: dies to uniform; 2: simple stable/periodic patterns; 3: chaos (random-looking); 4: complex localised structures that move and interact.
  • Class 4 sits between order and chaos. Structures persist long enough to carry information and interact to process it, which is why Rule 110 can perform universal computation.

questions.q: A live cell has 4 live neighbours. A dead cell has 2. What happens to each?

opts.t: The live cell dies (overcrowding); the dead cell stays dead
The live cell survives; the dead cell comes alive

questions.why: Survival needs 2 or 3 neighbours, so 4 is too many. Birth needs exactly 3, so 2 is not enough.

questions.title: Count the glider's cells
questions.tests: assert counts == [5] * 8, f"A glider keeps exactly 5 live cells at every step, got {counts}"

questions.q: Someone says: "Gliders aren't real. There are only cells turning on and off." Which point answers that?

opts.t: They're right; higher-level descriptions are errors
"Glider" is a valid, useful higher-level description, and the debate over whether it's "real" is the realism vs instrumentalism question
Gliders are real because they're in the source code
The rules of Life explicitly define gliders

questions.why: Nothing in the two rules mentions gliders, yet "a glider moves one cell diagonally every 4 steps" predicts the system perfectly. Whether such emergent objects are "real" is exactly what realists and instrumentalists disagree about.

questions.q: Explain the kernel-10 trick: why is "alive next step" the same as "c is 3, 12 or 13"?
questions.a:
• The kernel adds up the 8 neighbours with weight 1 and the cell itself with weight 10, so c = 10·self + neighbours.
  • Dead cells have c = 0…8; live cells have c = 10…18. The two ranges can't overlap.
  • Birth (dead, 3 neighbours) → 3. Survival (alive, 2 or 3) → 12 or 13. Any other value means dead next step.

questions.q: What did the glider gun prove, and why does it matter for complexity science?
questions.a:
• Conway conjectured that every finite starting pattern eventually stops growing. The gun is a finite pattern whose population grows forever (one glider every 30 steps), so the conjecture is false.
  • It shows you often can't predict what simple rules will do by reasoning about them: you have to run them. And guns are a building block for computation in Life (glider streams as signals).

lap = np.roll(a, 1) + np.roll(a, -1) - 2 * a
print(lap)
print(a + 0.1 * lap)

questions.q: After the diffusion step in the prediction, what's true about the total amount of ink?

opts.t: It's unchanged: what leaves the peak arrives at its neighbours
It decreases, because the peak shrank
It increases, because two cells gained

questions.why: The Laplacian sums to zero over a wrapping grid (every bit that leaves one cell enters a neighbour), so diffusion conserves the total. Check: the values in the second row still add to 9.

questions.q: The jump from "almost never" to "almost always" percolating is centred near q ≈ 0.593 and gets sharper for bigger grids. Where have you seen this shape before?

opts.t: The connectivity of Erdős–Rényi graphs in chapter 2
The degree distribution of BA graphs

questions.why: Both are phase transitions: a global property (connected graph / percolating rock) switches on abruptly at a critical value of a local probability. The Map of Ideas links them for this reason.

counts = 3 * sizes ** 2
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log(sizes), np.log(counts), 1)
print(round(slope, 3))

questions.q: Describe the percolation model and what "critical porosity" means.
questions.a:
• An n×n grid; each cell porous with probability q. Water starts in the top row and repeatedly spreads to porous neighbours.
  • The rock percolates if water reaches the bottom row.
  • Below about q = 0.593 large grids almost never percolate; above it they almost always do. That threshold is the critical value of a phase transition, and the transition gets sharper as n grows.

questions.q: What does a fractal dimension of about 1.85 mean for the wet cluster, and how do you measure it?
questions.a:
• The number of wet cells grows like n^1.85 as the grid grows: faster than a line (n¹), slower than a filled square (n²). The cluster has holes at every scale.
  • Measure it by counting cells for several sizes and fitting a straight line to log(count) vs log(n); the slope is the dimension.

questions.q: A pile full of 3s, everywhere. You drop one grain in the centre. What happens?

opts.t: A huge avalanche that can sweep most of the grid

questions.why: Every neighbour is already at 3, so each topple pushes neighbours to 4 and they topple too. The avalanche spreads across the whole grid until grains fall off the edges. A system at its limit everywhere is fragile.

questions.title: drop
questions.prompt: Rebuild drop(a, rng): add one grain at a random cell, relax, and return the avalanche's (duration, size).
questions.tests:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = np.zeros((4, 4), dtype=int)
assert drop(a, rng) == (0, 0) and a.sum() == 1

questions.q: Most drops cause no avalanche at all, yet some cause hundreds of topples. On log-log axes, the CCDF of sizes falls roughly in a straight line over a wide range. What's the term for that?
questions.why: A straight line on log-log axes means the chance of a bigger avalanche falls off like a power of its size, not exponentially. There's no "typical" avalanche size; huge ones are rare but not vanishingly rare. That's the signature of criticality.

questions.q: After a huge avalanche, someone asks "which grain caused it?" What does the SOC view say?

opts.t: The grain was only the trigger; the real cause is the pile's critical state, which made a large avalanche possible

questions.why: In a critical system the size of the response is set by the state of the whole pile, not by the trigger. Asking which grain caused it is like asking which match caused a forest fire after decades of dry undergrowth.

questions.q: What makes the sand pile "self-organized" critical, compared with percolation at q = 0.593?
questions.a:
• In percolation, the critical point is a parameter value someone has to choose.
  • The sand pile reaches its critical state by itself: slow driving (one grain at a time) plus fast relaxation (avalanches) pushes it to the state where avalanches of all sizes occur.
  • Evidence: the average height settles near 2.1 whatever the start, and avalanche sizes and durations follow heavy-tailed distributions.

questions.q: Describe the drop-and-relax experiment and what you measure.
questions.a:
• Start with a tall pile and relax it to stability.
  • Repeatedly add one grain at a random cell and relax, counting the steps (duration) and total topples (size) of each avalanche.
  • Plot the distributions of size and duration on log-log axes (PMF or CCDF). A roughly straight line across a wide range is the heavy tail.

questions.q: With p = 0.3, each agent is content when only 30% of its neighbours match. Segregation still jumps from about 0.5 to about 0.75. Why is this the headline result?

opts.t: Mild individual preferences produce strong collective segregation, so the outcome doesn't reveal what individuals want
It shows the model is broken

questions.why: The pattern at the level of the city overstates the preferences of the agents. You can't infer intent from the aggregate, a lesson that matters well beyond housing.

questions.title: An agent's step
questions.prompt: Rebuild the order of an agent's turn: move, harvest everything in the new cell, burn sugar, and report whether it starved.
questions.setup:
def best_cell(sugar, loc, vision, occupied):
    return loc

questions.q: Survivors are disproportionately agents with high vision and low metabolism. Is this selection, as in evolution?

opts.t: Yes, exactly the same as evolution
It's selection of who survives, but with no reproduction or inheritance, so it can't build up improvements over generations
No, because all agents start equal

questions.why: The population's average vision rises because poorly-equipped agents die, not because anyone's children inherit better eyes. Chapter 11 adds the missing ingredients: reproduction and variation.

questions.q: In Sugarscape no rule mentions wealth inequality. Explain how it emerges.
questions.a:
• Agents differ (heterogeneity): some see far and burn little sugar; others see little and burn a lot.
  • Location matters: agents near a mountain peak harvest more, and good foragers find and hold the peaks.
  • Advantages compound: sugar left over each step accumulates, while poorly-equipped agents hover near zero or die.
  • So a skewed (long right tail) wealth distribution emerges from individual differences plus the landscape, with no rule about wealth.

questions.q: List the four features that describe agent-based models.
questions.a:
• Agents that model individuals with their own state and behaviour.
  • Heterogeneity: agents differ from each other.
  • An environment the agents move through and change.
  • Local interactions: agents sense and act on their surroundings, not the whole world.

questions.q: Cars all drive forward. Can a traffic jam (the region of slow cars) move backward?

opts.t: No, a jam is made of cars, so it moves with them
Yes: cars leave the front of the jam and new cars join at the back, so the jam itself drifts backward

questions.why: The jam is a pattern, not a set of cars. Cars exit at its front (speeding up) while new cars arrive at its back (braking), so the pattern travels upstream even though every car moves forward. Like the glider, it's an emergent object.

questions.code:
locs = np.array([10, 40, 90])
L = 100
ahead = np.roll(locs, -1)
print(ahead)
print((ahead - locs) % L)

questions.title: One car's turn
questions.tests:
assert gap == 30, f"The car ahead is 30 cells away, round the ring: got {gap}"
assert speed == 11 and me == 1, f"Plenty of room, so speed up to 11 and wrap past the end to cell 1. Got speed {speed}, position {me}"

questions.q: Explain why one driver briefly braking can create a jam that lasts and moves backward.
questions.a:
• The car behind sees a smaller gap and must slow down too, slightly later; then the car behind it, and so on. The slowdown propagates upstream.
  • Each car takes time to accelerate back up, so cars leave the front of the slow region more slowly than new cars arrive at its back when traffic is dense.
  • The slow region (the jam) is a pattern that moves backward, even though every car moves forward.

questions.q: Name the three Boids rules, and say what's surprising about the result.
questions.a:
• Cohesion (toward neighbours' centre), separation (away from boids that are too close), alignment (match neighbours' average heading).
  • Every rule is local and there's no leader, yet the group moves as a coherent flock that splits and merges around obstacles. The flock is emergent.

questions.q: A population copies itself perfectly (no mutation) and some genotypes reproduce faster than others. What happens over a long time?

opts.t: The best genotype already present takes over, then nothing changes

questions.why: Selection only chooses among existing variants. Without new variation the fittest starting genotype eventually dominates and evolution stops. You'll see this in the simulation.

questions.code:
one_values  = np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.5])
zero_values = np.array([0.2, 0.7, 0.5])
loc = np.array([1, 1, 0])
print(np.where(loc, one_values, zero_values))
print(round(np.mean(np.where(loc, one_values, zero_values)), 3))

questions.q: In this landscape, how many genotypes are there with N = 8, and is there one best genotype?

opts.t: 256; yes, the one that picks the larger value at every position

questions.why: Each position independently prefers 0 or 1, so the best genome takes the better choice everywhere. It's a smooth landscape with a single peak, which makes it a clean test of selection and mutation.

questions.title: One generation
questions.prompt: Rebuild a generation of the simulation: score everyone, choose who dies at random, replace them with (possibly mutated) copies of agents chosen by fitness.
lines: def generation(pop, landscape, rng, death_rate=0.1, p_mutate=0.05):
fits = np.array([landscape.fitness(g) for g in pop])
for d, p in zip(dead, parents):
distractors: fits = np.array([landscape.fitness(g) for g in dead])

questions.q: "No mutation, random start" rises quickly and then goes flat below the best possible fitness, while "no mutation, identical start" never moves at all. Why?

opts.t: Selection used up the variation that was there at the start; with no new variants it can't climb higher
Mutation is required for any change at all

questions.why: With a random start there's plenty of variation, so selection improves fitness at first. Once the population converges on the best of what existed, there's nothing new to select. With an identical start there's no variation at all, so selection has nothing to act on. Mutation supplies the novelty that keeps the climb going.

questions.q: "No selection" drifts up from the worst genome to about the middle (roughly 0.5) and then wanders, far below the peak. Which ingredient is missing?

opts.t: Replication; the population can't copy itself
Differential reproduction; without it, mutation just causes random drift, not adaptation
Nothing is missing; this is normal evolution

questions.why: Copies and mutations still happen, so the population changes, but nothing favours fitter variants. It drifts toward a typical random genome (average fitness), not toward the peak. Adaptation needs selection and variation together.

questions.q: What are the three ingredients of evolution in the minimal view, and what happens when you remove variation or selection?
questions.a:
• Replicators, variation, differential survival or reproduction.
  • No variation (no mutation): selection quickly picks the best existing genotype, then fitness stops rising.
  • No selection: mutation causes random drift; fitness wanders but doesn't climb.
  • Only with all three does the population keep adapting toward a peak.

questions.q: Why choose replacements with probability proportional to fitness instead of always copying the single best agent?
questions.a:
• It models differential reproduction realistically: fitter agents tend to have more offspring, but luck still matters.
  • It keeps variation in the population longer, so evolution can explore instead of collapsing onto one genotype immediately.

questions.q: In a single round, the other player defects. What's your best response, and what if they cooperate?

opts.t: Defect in both cases: 1 > 0 if they defect, and 5 > 3 if they cooperate
It depends on the other player's strategy

questions.why: Defection is a dominant strategy in a one-shot game: it's better whatever the other player does. That's what makes it a dilemma: two players following this logic both end up with 1 instead of 3.

questions.code:
genome = ["C", "C", "D", "C", "D", "C", "D"]
for hist in [[], ["D"], ["C", "D"], ["D", "D", "C"]]:
    key = "".join(hist[-2:])
    print(repr(key), genome[KEYS.index(key)])

questions.q: Tit for tat never scores more than its opponent in a single match (it lost 5–10 to all-D). Yet in Axelrod's 1980 tournaments it had the highest total score. How?

opts.t: It does well against cooperators (18 each) and loses only a little to defectors, so its average across all opponents is high
It beats every strategy head to head

questions.why: Head-to-head wins don't matter; total points across all games do. All-D beats everyone it meets, but scores poorly overall because nobody cooperates with it. Tit for tat earns full cooperation from nice strategies and limits its losses against nasty ones.

questions.title: Who wins head to head?
lines: winner = "tit for tat" if s_tft > s_d else "always D"

questions.q: Why can a mutant cooperator in an all-defector population not take off alone, while a small cluster of reciprocators can?

opts.t: A lone cooperator only meets defectors and gets exploited; reciprocators that meet each other earn 18 instead of 6 and outscore defectors
Defectors refuse to play with cooperators

questions.why: Cooperation pays only when cooperators meet each other. That's why it often appears in waves: a few reciprocators drift in, find each other, out-earn defectors, and spread.

questions.q: Explain how cooperation can evolve in a population that starts out all defectors, using the iterated prisoner's dilemma.
questions.a:
• In a single game defection dominates, but in repeated games strategies can condition on history.
  • Mutation occasionally produces reciprocating strategies (nice but retaliating, like tit for tat).
  • When reciprocators meet each other they cooperate and earn far more than defectors earn against each other (18 vs 6 over 6 rounds), while losing little against defectors.
  • Fitness-proportional reproduction spreads them, so niceness and average score rise, often in waves, without anyone being altruistic.

questions.q: List Axelrod's traits of successful strategies.
questions.a: • Nice (never defect first), retaliating (punish defection), forgiving (return to cooperation), and clear (easy for others to read).
